title: Chapter 11 — Nightgown
paragraphs: We had lain in bed chatting and napping in short intervals, with Queequeg now and then affectionately throwing his brown tattooed legs over mine and drawing them back. We were entirely relaxed and comfortable. At last, our conversation chased away the last traces of sleepiness, and we felt like getting up — though dawn was still some way off.

We grew so wide awake that lying down became tiresome. Little by little we sat up, bedclothes tucked snugly around us, leaning against the headboard with our four knees drawn up close together and our two noses bent over them, as if our kneecaps were warming pans. We felt wonderfully cozy, especially since it was so cold outside — and outside the blankets too, since there was no fire in the room. To truly enjoy bodily warmth, some small part of you must be cold, because no quality in this world exists except by contrast. Nothing exists in itself. If you believe you've been perfectly comfortable for a long time, then you can no longer be said to be comfortable at all. But if, like Queequeg and me in that bed, only the tip of your nose or the crown of your head is slightly chilled, then in your general consciousness you feel most deliciously warm. For this reason, a bedroom should never have a fire — that's one of the luxurious discomforts of the rich. The height of this kind of bliss is having nothing but the blanket between your warmth and the cold outside air. Then you lie like the one warm spark in the heart of an arctic crystal.

We had been sitting hunched like this for some time when I decided to open my eyes. When I'm between sheets, day or night, awake or asleep, I tend to keep my eyes shut to concentrate the feeling of being in bed. Because no person can truly feel their own identity unless their eyes are closed — as if darkness were the proper element of our essence, though light suits our clay better. Opening my eyes and leaving my own pleasant, self-created darkness for the imposed outer gloom of an unlit midnight, I felt a disagreeable jolt. Nor did I object when Queequeg suggested we light a lamp, since we were wide awake and he badly wanted a few quiet puffs from his tomahawk pipe. I should mention that although I'd been so against his smoking in bed the night before, see how elastic our stiff prejudices become once love starts to bend them. Now I liked nothing better than having Queequeg smoke beside me — even in bed — because he seemed so full of serene, domestic contentment. I no longer worried about the landlord's fire insurance. I was alive only to the condensed, confidential comfort of sharing a pipe and a blanket with a real friend. With our shaggy jackets around our shoulders, we passed the tomahawk pipe back and forth until a blue canopy of smoke slowly gathered above us, lit by the flame of the newly lit lamp.

Whether that undulating canopy of smoke carried the savage away to distant scenes, I don't know, but he began speaking of his native island. Eager to hear his story, I asked him to go on. He gladly agreed. Though at the time I barely understood half his words, later conversations — when I'd grown more familiar with his broken English — now allow me to present the whole story, such as it is, in the bare skeleton I give here.
